clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A nurse is preparing to access a subcutaneous implanted venous port. Which equipment and technique are appropriate?

options.A: Cleanse the site with an appropriate antiseptic and insert a sterile non-coring (Huber) needle using aseptic technique.
options.B: Cleanse the site, then access the port septum with a standard hypodermic needle using clean technique.
options.C: Insert a peripheral IV catheter through the port septum after cleansing the overlying skin.
options.D: Use a non-coring needle but omit site antisepsis when the overlying skin appears visibly clean.

semantic_correction.rationale: FDA classifies the non-coring (Huber) needle as a sterile needle designed to access a subcutaneous implanted intravascular infusion port without damaging the septum. CDC outpatient-oncology infection-control guidance directs clinicians to perform hand hygiene, cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, and insert a non-coring needle while maintaining aseptic technique. A standard hypodermic needle, a peripheral IV catheter, or omission of site antisepsis does not match the recommended port-access method.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Access an implanted venous port using appropriate skin antisepsis, aseptic technique, and a sterile non-coring (Huber) needle designed for the port septum.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original correct answer was uniquely longest. The revised item tests the same device-specific access method with concise parallel alternatives and current FDA classification evidence.

option_audit.A: Correct. It combines the FDA-designated non-coring needle with CDC-recommended site antisepsis and aseptic port access.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. A standard hypodermic needle is not the FDA-designated non-coring device for implanted port access.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. A peripheral IV catheter is not the device used to puncture and access an implanted port septum.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. CDC guidance includes cleansing the port site with an appropriate antiseptic before needle insertion.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone contains both the correct port-access needle and the required antisepsis/aseptic technique.
cueing_check: All four choices are concrete port-access approaches of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
